readingInstruction: Read Psalm 136. Every verse ends with the same refrain: “for his steadfast love endures forever.” Read it aloud if you can, as a litany, with the second half as a response.
settingTheScene: Psalm 136 is called the Great Hallel in Jewish tradition and is sung at Passover. It is a liturgy: one voice would say the first line, and the congregation would respond with the refrain. It recounts creation and the exodus and the conquest in the language of God’s steadfast love. After Daniel’s stories, it is a fitting close to Unit 13’s reading of the exile: the God who is sovereign over empires is the God whose love endures forever. It will return later in the plan.
observation: “Give thanks to the LORD, for he is good, for his steadfast love endures forever” (v. 1).
“Give thanks to the God of gods, for his steadfast love endures forever” (v. 2).
“To him who alone does great wonders, for his steadfast love endures forever” (v. 4).
“To him who by understanding made the heavens, for his steadfast love endures forever” (v. 5).
“To him who struck down the firstborn of Egypt, for his steadfast love endures forever” (v. 10).
“To him who divided the Red Sea in two” (v. 13).
“It is he who remembered us in our low estate, for his steadfast love endures forever” (v. 23).
“He who gives food to all flesh, for his steadfast love endures forever” (v. 25).
interpretation:
The refrain, repeated twenty-six times, is the heart of the psalm. “His steadfast love endures forever.” The Hebrew word hesed, covenant love, is the theme. The psalm teaches that every act of God, in creation, in redemption, and in daily provision, flows from this love.

The structure is a story. The first section is creation: God made the heavens by understanding, spread out the earth, and made the great lights. The sun rules the day, and the moon and stars the night. The creation is not an accident or a conflict but a gift of love. The second section is redemption: God struck down the firstborn of Egypt, brought out Israel with a strong hand, divided the sea, and led his people through the wilderness. Even the destruction of the enemy kings is told as part of this love. The point is not cruelty but faithfulness to the covenant. The third section is the land given as a heritage.

Then there is a turn in verse 23: “It is he who remembered us in our low estate.” This is likely about the exile and the return. In the lowest point of the people’s history, God did not forget. And so the psalm ends with the universal provision of God: “He who gives food to all flesh,” and a final call: “Give thanks to the God of heaven, for his steadfast love endures forever.”

Reading Psalm 136 after the book of Lamentations is powerful. In Lamentations 3:22, the poet says, “The steadfast love of the LORD never ceases.” Here it is made into a song. After a unit about judgment, exile, and the fall of nations, the closing word is not wrath but love that endures.
connection: 1 John 4:8 says, “God is love.” Romans 8:38-39 says nothing can separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord. Ephesians 2:4-5 says, “God, being rich in mercy, because of the great love with which he loved us, even when we were dead in our trespasses, made us alive.” John 3:16 shows God’s love in giving his Son. Matthew 26:30 says that Jesus and his disciples sang a hymn after the Last Supper, probably the Hallel.
application:
Pray Psalm 136 as a litany, aloud, with a friend or family member. One person reads the first line, and the other answers the refrain.

Add your own verses: “To him who … for his steadfast love endures forever.” Name three things from your own life.

Remember a time God “remembered you in your low estate.”
prayerPrompts: Give thanks to God, line by line, for his steadfast love in your own story.
Remember how he remembered you in your low estate.
Give thanks to the God of heaven.
